title: Refactoring to Fix Smells
summary: The standard toolkit for turning a smelly method into clean ones safely — Extract Method, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Introduce Parameter Object — and the tests that make it safe.

slides.markdown:
Spotting a smell (see [Common Code Smells](common-code-smells)) is half the job — the other half is fixing it without breaking anything. **Refactoring** is a specific, disciplined kind of change: restructure the code's internals while its observable behavior stays identical, verified by tests at every step.

This topic covers the small number of refactors that fix most smells — Extract Method, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, Introduce Parameter Object — and the one rule that makes all of them safe: never refactor code you can't verify.

slides.sectionTitle: Refactoring: behavior-preserving change, and why tests are the safety net
slides.markdown:
**Refactoring** means changing a program's internal structure without changing what it does — same inputs still produce the same outputs. This is the property that separates refactoring from "rewriting": a rewrite is free to change behavior; a refactor is explicitly not.

That guarantee is only as good as your ability to verify it, which is why tests are the safety net, not an optional nicety. Without tests, "I refactored this and it still works" is a claim based on reading the diff carefully — which is exactly how subtle behavior changes slip through undetected. With tests passing before and after, the same claim is backed by evidence.

slides.sectionTitle: Extract Method and Extract Class: the two workhorse refactors
slides.markdown:
**Extract Method** takes a chunk of a long method — a loop, a calculation, a validation block — and gives it its own name as a separate method. It directly fixes long-method smell, and it's usually the first move on any smelly function, because naming the chunk immediately clarifies what it does without reading its body.

**Extract Class** does the same thing one level up: when a class has accumulated fields and methods that form a natural sub-group (say, everything related to an order's shipping address), pull them into their own class that the original class now holds a reference to. It's the direct fix for a Large Class smell drifting toward a God Object.

Both refactors are low-risk precisely because they don't change logic — they only change where it lives and what it's called.

slides.sectionTitle: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: killing a type-check switch
slides.markdown:
A recurring smell is a `switch` or chain of `if/else` branching on a type field — `if (shape.type == CIRCLE) ... else if (shape.type == SQUARE) ...` — repeated in multiple methods across the codebase. Every time a new type is added, every one of those switch statements needs a new branch, and it's easy to miss one.

**Replace Conditional with Polymorphism** turns each branch into an override on a subclass: `Circle.area()`, `Square.area()`, each implementing its own logic, called through one shared interface. Adding a new shape means adding one new subclass with its own `area()` method — no existing switch statement needs to be found and edited at all. This is the same idea behind object-oriented design's open/closed principle: existing code stays closed to modification, new behavior extends it instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: before/after of replacing a conditional with a Strategy object
slides.markdown:
![Before: one calculateShipping method with an inline if-else chain. After: a ShippingCalculator interface with StandardShipping, ExpressShipping, OvernightShipping classes called via context.calculate()](assets/refactoring-shipping.svg)

The before/after makes the trade visible: the branching didn't disappear, it moved from one crowded method into several small classes, each responsible for exactly one case.

The payoff shows up on the next new shipping type: it's a new class, not a new branch to remember inside an existing method.

slides.sectionTitle: Introduce Parameter Object: fixing a long parameter list
slides.markdown:
When several parameters travel together across multiple method signatures — `startDate, endDate, timezone` appearing in `scheduleEvent`, `checkAvailability`, and `sendReminder` — **Introduce Parameter Object** bundles them into one type, `DateRange`, and every method takes that instead of three loose values.

This is the same move as fixing a data clump (see [Common Code Smells](common-code-smells)), applied specifically to parameters: it shortens signatures, and it gives you one place to add validation (`endDate` after `startDate`) that used to need repeating, or forgetting, at every call site.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a step-by-step refactor of a smelly method into three clean ones
Pitfall: refactoring without characterization tests first
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This method is a mess, but I understand what it does well enough to restructure it directly."

**Why it's wrong:** "understanding what it does" from reading is not the same as verifying it — smelly legacy methods often have edge cases (an empty list, a null customer, a boundary date) that aren't obvious from a read-through but are exercised in production. Refactor by reading alone, and you can silently change behavior for exactly the inputs you didn't think to check.

**Correct model:** before restructuring code with no tests, write a **characterization test** — one that asserts on the method's *current* actual outputs for a range of inputs, including the edge cases you can find, without judging whether that behavior is correct. It's a scaffold, not a spec: it exists so any refactor that changes behavior fails loudly, immediately, instead of shipping silently.

slides.sectionTitle: How to talk through a live refactor in an interview
slides.markdown:
When an interviewer hands you smelly code and asks you to clean it up live, the strongest signal isn't the final diff — it's the order of operations. Narrate the plan before typing: name the smells you see, state which refactor fixes each one, and say what you'd verify before and after.

A strong sequence sounds like: "I see a long method mixing validation and pricing, and a type-check switch on tier — I'd extract the validation and pricing into their own methods first, run the existing tests, then replace the tier switch with polymorphism, and run tests again after each step, not just at the end." That sequencing — small steps, verified individually — is what interviewers are actually screening for, more than whether you land on the textbook-perfect final structure.
